subject: Biochemistry
vignette: A 41-year-old man with central obesity and type 2 diabetes mellitus has a fasting triglyceride level of 1150 mg/dL and normal LDL cholesterol; he has no xanthomas. Lipoprotein lipase activity and LDL receptor function are normal, and his liver shows increased VLDL secretion.
question: Which of the following is the most likely cause of his hypertriglyceridemia?
explanation_correct: Familial hypertriglyceridemia (type IV dyslipidemia) is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by hepatic overproduction of VLDL, which is closely related to insulin resistance and increased hepatic fatty acid synthesis. Triglyceride levels above 1000 mg/dL predispose to acute pancreatitis.

explanation_incorrect.A: Lipoprotein lipase deficiency causes type I hyperchylomicronemia with chylomicrons, a creamy supernatant, eruptive xanthomas, and pancreatitis.
explanation_incorrect.B: Apo CII deficiency also produces the type I phenotype because lipoprotein lipase cannot be activated.
explanation_incorrect.C: A defect in the LDL receptor causes familial hypercholesterolemia (type II) with elevated LDL cholesterol and tendon xanthomas.
explanation_incorrect.D: Apo E deficiency causes type III dysbetalipoproteinemia with mixed hyperlipidemia and palmar or tuberoeruptive xanthomas.

educationalObjective: Type IV familial hypertriglyceridemia reflects hepatic overproduction of VLDL and is associated with insulin resistance.
